text:
The Long Way Home

On the afternoon of April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rocket lifted off from Kennedy Space Center carrying three men toward the Moon. Apollo 13 was meant to be the third lunar landing, and by then the public had begun to treat such journeys as routine. Jim Lovell, the commander, had already flown to the Moon once on Apollo 8. Fred Haise would pilot the lunar module, which was named Aquarius. The command module pilot was Jack Swigert, who had joined the crew only days earlier. The original pilot, Ken Mattingly, had been exposed to German measles and was grounded by flight surgeons, and Swigert took his place after a hurried round of training.

The first two days went so smoothly that the crew nearly bored the television audience. They coasted outward in the command module, called Odyssey, and even gave a broadcast showing the inside of their spacecraft. Few networks bothered to carry it. Nobody on the ground or in space suspected that a flaw had been waiting inside the spacecraft since before launch.

That flaw lay in one of two oxygen tanks in the service module, the cylinder of equipment attached to the back of the command module. Years before, the tank had been dropped slightly during handling. Later, during ground testing, technicians had trouble draining it, and they used heaters to boil off the oxygen. The heaters were protected by thermostat switches built for 28 volts, yet the ground power supply ran at 65 volts. The switches fused shut, the temperature inside climbed to hundreds of degrees, and the Teflon insulation on the internal wiring was quietly cooked away. No one noticed. The tank passed its checks and flew.

About 56 hours into the flight, and roughly 200,000 miles from Earth, controllers in Houston asked the crew to stir the cryogenic tanks, a routine step that keeps the contents from stratifying. Swigert flipped the switch. Moments later, just after nine at night in Houston, the crew heard a loud bang and felt the ship shudder. A spark had jumped across the bare wires in the damaged tank, and the oxygen had ignited. Swigert reported that they had a problem. Lovell repeated it, and the line has since become part of the language.

At first the crew and controllers thought they faced an instrument fault. Warning lights told a different story. Voltage on the main electrical buses was falling. One oxygen tank was empty and the other was draining fast. Looking out the window, Lovell saw gas streaming into space. That told him what no gauge could. The spacecraft was losing its supply of oxygen, and without oxygen the fuel cells could not make electricity or water. The Moon landing was gone. The question now was whether the three men would survive.

In Houston, flight director Gene Kranz gathered his team and pushed them to think about what the ship still had. The answer lay in the lunar module attached to the front of the stack. Aquarius had its own batteries, its own oxygen and its own engine. It was designed to keep two men alive for two days on the Moon. Now it would have to sustain three men for nearly four days. The crew moved into it as the command module was shut down to save its remaining battery power, which would be needed for the return to Earth.

Swigert and Haise crowded into the small cabin with Lovell. The ship's course was a further concern. The original path would not bring them home. Controllers chose to swing the spacecraft around the far side of the Moon on a path that used lunar gravity to sling it back toward Earth. To fix that path, Aquarius fired its descent engine for a burn that turned the lunar lander into a rescue tug. Later burns refined the aim and sped up the return, so that the crew would arrive earlier and with fewer consumables to stretch.

As they passed behind the Moon, the crew reached a point farther from Earth than any humans had ever traveled, almost 250,000 miles away. They had no time to savor the record. Lovell looked down at the gray surface he had hoped to walk on, then turned back to the work of staying alive.

Life in the little lander grew harder by the hour. To conserve power, the crew switched off nearly everything, including the heating. The cabin temperature sank toward freezing, and moisture condensed on the walls. Water was rationed to a few ounces per man each day. Haise developed a fever and a painful infection, and Lovell and Swigert slept in snatches, if at all. Meanwhile, the real engineering battle went on in Houston.

The most dangerous problem was carbon dioxide. The air in a closed cabin fills with the gas the crew exhales, and Aquarius had only enough filter canisters for two men for a short stay. The command module had plenty of spare canisters, but they were square and the receptacles in the lunar module were round. Engineers on the ground gathered the items the crew had on board, including plastic bags, cardboard from a flight manual cover, a spacesuit hose and a roll of duct tape. They designed an adapter and read the instructions to the crew over the radio. The crew assembled it, and the carbon dioxide level began to fall. The makeshift device worked.

Another team, led partly by the sidelined Ken Mattingly, worked in a simulator to write a procedure for starting up the command module in the right order after days of cold storage. Power had to be rationed so tightly that the battery would last through reentry. Mattingly tested sequence after sequence until he found one that fit within the budget, and the instructions were read up to the crew.

As the spacecraft neared Earth, the crew made a final course correction. Without their usual navigation systems, they aligned the ship using the line between day and night on the Earth below. Then they separated the damaged service module. Looking at it as it drifted away, they saw that an entire panel had been blown off and the side was scorched. The photographs they took would later help investigators understand what had happened.

Last, they climbed back into Odyssey and released Aquarius, which had saved their lives and would now burn up in the atmosphere. Reentry brought a communications blackout that lasted longer than expected. In Houston, controllers waited in silence. Then voices came through, and parachutes opened over the South Pacific. Odyssey splashed down on April 17, near Samoa, and the crew were lifted aboard the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima. They were thinner, thirsty and tired, but alive.

Investigators later traced the explosion to the tank's history, to the damage done during ground testing and to the mismatched thermostats. NASA redesigned the tank and its wiring, and added a third oxygen tank on later flights. Apollo 13 never reached the Moon, yet many people regard it as one of the great achievements of the space program. It showed that engineers and astronauts, working together under pressure, could turn a catastrophe into a safe return. Lovell later called the mission a successful failure, and that phrase fits it well.
